title: If / Else
intro: `if` needs no parentheses around the condition. It is also an expression, so it can produce a value.

coming_from.go: `if` looks like Go's: no parentheses, braces required, and the condition must be a `bool`. It is also an expression, so `let size = if n > 5 { "big" } else { "small" };` replaces declaring `size` first and assigning in a branch.
coming_from.kotlin: This is Kotlin's `if` expression without the parentheses, and the braces are required. Both branches must give the same type, where Kotlin would quietly pick a common supertype.
coming_from.python: `if` with a value replaces `"big" if n > 5 else "small"`. The condition must be a real `bool`: there is no truthiness, so `if n` with a number or `if items` with a list won't compile.
coming_from.typescript: `if` with a value replaces the ternary `n > 5 ? "big" : "small"`. The condition must be a real `bool`, so `if n` with a number or `if s` with a string won't compile, and both branches must give the same type.
coming_from.java: Rust's `if` is an expression, so `let size = if n > 5 { "big" } else { "small" };` replaces the `?:` ternary, which Rust does not have. Rust never converts one branch to fit the other, where Java's ternary would pick a common supertype or promote a number.
coming_from.csharp: `if` gives back a value, so it replaces C#'s `?:`, which Rust does not have. Like C#, the condition must be a `bool`; unlike C#'s `?:`, Rust never converts one branch to fit the other. Rust also drops the parentheses but always needs the braces.
coming_from.c: Rust's `if` is an expression that replaces `?:`, which Rust does not have. The condition must be a real `bool` (no `if (n)` on an integer or pointer), and both branches must have the same type, so a `0` can't stand in for a null string.
coming_from.cpp: `if` is an expression, so it does the job of `?:`, which Rust does not have. The condition must be a `bool`, with no implicit conversion from integers or pointers, and both branches must have exactly the same type.

notes: The condition must be a `bool`. `if n { }` with a number does not compile. There is no "truthy" zero, so write `if n != 0`.
There is no ternary `a ? b : c`. `if a { b } else { c }` is the same thing.
Chain tests with `else if`. When every branch compares one value against fixed cases, `match` (a later lesson) is usually clearer.
`if let` and `let ... else` test whether a value has a given shape and name its parts in the same step. They replace "check, then unpack".
`&&` and `||` stop as soon as the answer is known, so the right side runs only when it is needed.

gotcha.title: Two branches that give different types
gotcha.looks_fine: Kotlin accepts this and gives `size` a loose common type (`Comparable<*> & Serializable`). Go has no `if` expression, so you would never write it.
gotcha.rust_sees: Rust gives every variable exactly one type, decided while compiling. `size` cannot be "a string or maybe a number".
gotcha.why: Code after this line uses `size`. If it could be either type, every later line would need to check which one it got. Rust makes both branches agree up front instead. If you really want "string or number", that is an enum, covered later.

go.says: Go has no `if` expression, so this can't come up. You declare `size` with one type first and assign to it in each branch.

kotlin.says: Kotlin runs this and prints big. `size` quietly gets a loose common type instead of `String`, so later code can't use it as text without a check.

python.says: Python runs this and prints big. The two branches can give different types, so `size` might be a string or an int and later code has to cope with both.
python.code:
n = 7
size = "big" if n > 5 else 0
print(size)

typescript.says: Prints big. TypeScript infers the union `"big" | 0` and lets it through; every later use of `size` as a string then needs a `typeof` check or the compiler rejects it. Rust asks you to say so up front instead.

java.says: Java compiles this and prints big. It picks a shared supertype for the two branches, so `size` ends up as a vague Object-like type that later code can't do much with.

csharp.says: C# refuses this too: the two sides of `?:` must share a type, and there is no conversion between string and int (CS0173).
csharp.error: Program.cs(2,12): error CS0173: Type of conditional expression cannot be determined because there is no implicit conversion between 'string' and 'int'

c.says: C accepts this because a plain 0 counts as a null pointer. It prints big here, but with a smaller `n` the string would be NULL.

cpp.says: This compiles because a literal `0` also counts as a null pointer, so both branches become `const char*`. It prints `big`, but if `n` were small `cout` would get a null pointer.

truthy.py.code:
print("0 or 5:", 0 or 5)
print("[] or 'empty':", [] or "empty")
print("'a' and 'b':", "a" and "b")
print("1 < 3 < 5:", 1 < 3 < 5)
d = {"a": 0}
print('d.get("a") or 9:', d.get("a") or 9)
print('d.get("a", 9):', d.get("a", 9))
if []:
    print("a list is true")
else:
    print("an empty list is false")
